title: Magnet and its poles
subject: physics
definition: A magnet is an object that attracts magnetic materials towards itself without being in physical contact with them. The most familiar form is the bar magnet -- a rectangular piece of magnetic material, usually made of iron, steel, or a special alloy, that has been magnetised so that it can pick up iron nails, pins, and small iron objects. The defining property of a magnet is that it exerts a force on magnetic materials even from a distance; this force is called magnetic force, and because it acts without contact, it is classified as a non-contact force. A magnet has two special regions called poles, located at its two ends, where the magnetic force is strongest. These two poles are named the north pole (N) and the south pole (S). The middle region of the magnet, between the two poles, has almost no attracting power -- this is the weakest part. One of the most important properties of a magnet is that it always has two poles: no matter how many times a magnet is cut, each piece will still have a north pole and a south pole; a single isolated pole (a monopole) does not exist in ordinary magnets. When a magnet is freely suspended by a thread or floated on a cork in water, it comes to rest pointing in the north-south direction -- the end that points towards the geographic north is called the north pole, and the end that points towards the geographic south is called the south pole. This property is the basis of the magnetic compass used for finding directions. A magnet attracts magnetic materials -- substances that are pulled towards a magnet. The three common magnetic materials are iron, nickel, and cobalt. Steel, which is mostly iron, can also be attracted and can be made into a permanent magnet. Substances that are not attracted by a magnet are called non-magnetic materials; common examples include wood, plastic, glass, rubber, paper, and copper. A simple activity to test a material is to bring a bar magnet near it: if the material is pulled towards the magnet, it is magnetic; if nothing happens, it is non-magnetic. To identify the two poles of a bar magnet, one can sprinkle iron filings on a sheet of paper placed over the magnet -- the filings cluster densely at the two ends (the poles) and scarcely stick to the middle, clearly showing the regions of strongest magnetic force.
eli5: A magnet is like an invisible hand that grabs iron things without touching them. It has two strong ends called poles -- a north pole and a south pole -- and a weak middle. If you hang a magnet by a string, it turns until it points north-south, like a compass needle. It pulls iron, nickel, and cobalt, but ignores wood, plastic, and glass.

misconceptions.correction: Only iron, nickel, and cobalt are strongly attracted by a magnet. Copper, aluminium, brass, and lead are metals but are non-magnetic. CISCE examiner reports have repeatedly observed that students fail to distinguish magnetic from non-magnetic materials and lose marks by listing "metal" as a magnetic substance. Always name the specific material, not the broad category.

misconceptions.belief: If you cut a magnet in half, one piece will have only a north pole and the other only a south pole.
misconceptions.correction: A magnet always has two poles. Cutting a bar magnet produces two smaller magnets, each with its own north and south pole. A single isolated pole (monopole) does not exist in ordinary magnets. Examiners have noted that students struggle with pole-related reasoning in later classes (magnetic field direction, vector addition of fields), and the root confusion often begins here at Class 6 with the mistaken belief that poles can be separated.

misconceptions.belief: The middle of a bar magnet is the strongest part because it is the biggest.
misconceptions.correction: The magnetic force is strongest at the two ends (the poles) and weakest at the middle. Sprinkling iron filings clearly shows dense clusters at the ends and almost nothing in the centre.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define a magnet and name its two poles.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A magnet is an object that attracts magnetic materials towards itself without being in physical contact with them. It exerts a magnetic force -- a non-contact force -- on substances like iron, nickel, and cobalt. A magnet has two poles, which are the regions of strongest magnetic force located at its two ends. These two poles are called the north pole (N) and the south pole (S). The end that points towards the geographic north when the magnet is freely suspended is the north pole, and the end that points towards the geographic south is the south pole. The middle region of the magnet, between the two poles, has almost no attracting power. No matter how a magnet is shaped or cut, it always possesses both a north pole and a south pole; a single isolated pole does not exist in ordinary magnets.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Explain why a freely suspended bar magnet comes to rest in the north-south direction.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A bar magnet has two poles -- a north pole and a south pole -- and these poles interact with the Earth's magnetic field. The Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet, with its magnetic south pole located near the geographic north and its magnetic north pole near the geographic south. When a bar magnet is freely suspended by a thread, it is free to rotate. The north pole of the magnet is attracted towards the Earth's magnetic south (which lies near geographic north), and the south pole of the magnet is attracted towards the Earth's magnetic north (near geographic south). As a result, the magnet rotates until it aligns itself along the north-south line and comes to rest in that direction. This property is the principle behind the magnetic compass used for finding directions. It is important to note that the magnet does not point exactly along the geographic north-south line because the magnetic poles and geographic poles are not at exactly the same spot, but for Class 6 purposes we say it rests in the north-south direction.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student states, "Copper is a metal, so it must be a magnetic material because magnets attract metals." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement is incorrect and reveals a common misconception. Being a metal does not automatically make a substance magnetic. Magnetic materials are specifically those substances that are attracted by a magnet, and only three are commonly studied at this level -- iron, nickel, and cobalt. Copper, although it is a metal, is not attracted by a magnet and is therefore classified as a non-magnetic material. Other metals such as aluminium, brass, lead, and zinc are also non-magnetic. The confusion arises because the three most familiar magnetic materials (iron, nickel, cobalt) are all metals, which leads students to over-generalise and assume all metals must be magnetic. A simple test settles the matter: bring a bar magnet near a copper wire or a copper coin -- there is no attraction, no matter how close the magnet is. Therefore the correct classification is: copper is a metal but a non-magnetic material. CISCE examiner reports have repeatedly flagged this exact error -- students writing "metal" as a magnetic substance instead of naming iron, nickel, or cobalt specifically. The lesson is to classify materials by testing them with a magnet, not by assuming from the broader category they belong to. A balanced view acknowledges that while most magnetic substances happen to be metals, the reverse -- that all metals are magnetic -- is false.

diagnosticQuestions.question: You are given a bar magnet and a mixture of objects -- an iron nail, a plastic button, a nickel coin, a glass marble, a cobalt strip, a wooden pencil, and a copper ring. Classify each as magnetic or non-magnetic and describe how you would identify the two poles of the bar magnet.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: To classify the objects, bring the bar magnet near each one in turn and observe whether it is pulled towards the magnet. The iron nail, the nickel coin, and the cobalt strip are attracted -- these are magnetic materials (iron, nickel, and cobalt being the three magnetic materials). The plastic button, the glass marble, the wooden pencil, and the copper ring are not attracted -- these are non-magnetic materials. Note that copper is a metal but is still non-magnetic, which is an important distinction. To identify the two poles of the bar magnet, suspend it freely by tying a thread around its middle and allowing it to rotate. After it comes to rest, the end pointing towards the geographic north is the north pole (N) and the end pointing towards the geographic south is the south pole (S). Alternatively, sprinkle iron filings on a sheet of paper placed over the magnet -- the filings cluster densely at the two ends (the poles) and scarcely stick to the middle, clearly marking the regions of strongest magnetic force.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple classroom activity to teach a Class 4 student what a magnet is, what its two poles are, and which materials are magnetic. Describe the materials you would use and the steps.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: I would set up a "magnet discovery table" with a bar magnet, a small pile of iron nails, a nickel coin, a piece of cobalt or a steel paperclip, a wooden block, a plastic ruler, a glass marble, a rubber eraser, a copper wire, a sheet of white paper, and a spool of iron filings. Step 1: I would ask the child to hold the bar magnet over the iron nails and watch them jump up -- this demonstrates that a magnet attracts iron without touching it, introducing the idea of a non-contact force. Step 2: I would dip the magnet into the iron filings and let the child see the thick clusters at the two ends and almost nothing in the middle -- this visually introduces the two poles (north and south) as the regions of strongest force. Step 3: I would suspend the magnet by a thread and let it settle, showing that it points north-south -- this introduces the directional property and the idea of a compass. Step 4: I would ask the child to test each object (iron nail, nickel coin, steel clip, wooden block, plastic ruler, glass marble, rubber, copper wire) by bringing the magnet near, and sort them into two boxes labelled "Magnetic" and "Non-magnetic." Step 5: I would close by asking the child to name the three magnetic materials (iron, nickel, cobalt) and two non-magnetic ones, reinforcing the vocabulary. This hands-on activity turns abstract definitions into direct sensory experience and builds the foundation for later study of magnetic fields in higher classes.

masteryCriteria: Can define a magnet as an object that attracts magnetic materials and state that it exerts a non-contact force; can identify the two poles as north pole (N) and south pole (S) -- the regions of strongest magnetic force at the two ends; can list iron, nickel, and cobalt as magnetic materials and give at least two non-magnetic examples (wood, plastic, glass); can state that a freely suspended magnet rests in the north-south direction and that a magnet always has two poles.

title: Attraction and repulsion between magnets
subject: physics
definition:
A magnet has two poles -- a north pole and a south pole -- and when two magnets are brought near each other, the way they interact depends entirely on which poles face one another. The fundamental rule of magnetism is that like poles repel and unlike poles attract. "Like poles" means two poles of the same kind facing each other: a north pole facing another north pole (N--N), or a south pole facing another south pole (S--S). In both these cases the magnets push apart, and this pushing force is called repulsion. "Unlike poles" means two poles of different kinds facing each other: a north pole facing a south pole (N--S), or a south pole facing a north pole (S--N). In these cases the magnets pull together, and this pulling force is called attraction. So a north pole attracts a south pole but repels another north pole, and a south pole attracts a north pole but repels another south pole.

The force between two magnets is a non-contact force -- it acts at a distance, meaning the magnets do not have to touch each other for the push or pull to be felt. You can feel this force when you bring two bar magnets close to each other but not quite touching: like poles produce an invisible "cushion" that resists being pushed together, while unlike poles seem to leap towards each other and snap together. The strength of the force increases as the magnets get closer and decreases as they move apart, but the direction (attract or repel) depends only on the orientation of the poles.

To predict whether two magnets will attract or repel, look at the poles that are facing each other. If both are north or both are south, predict repulsion -- the magnets will push apart. If one is north and the other is south, predict attraction -- the magnets will pull together. A standard activity to demonstrate this uses two bar magnets: suspend one bar magnet by a thread so it can rotate freely and settle in the north--south direction, then bring the second magnet near one end in different orientations. When a north pole is brought near the suspended magnet's north pole, the suspended magnet swings away -- repulsion. When a north pole is brought near the suspended magnet's south pole, the suspended magnet swings towards the approaching magnet -- attraction. Reversing the approaching magnet reverses the effect. Recording these observations in a table confirms the rule: like poles repel, unlike poles attract, and the force acts without contact.
eli5: Think of two magnets as having two ends -- a red end (north) and a blue end (south). When two same-coloured ends face each other, they act like two stubborn children pushing each other away -- that is repulsion. When different-coloured ends face each other, they act like two friends hugging and pulling together -- that is attraction. And they do all this without even touching, like magic invisible hands.

misconceptions.belief: All magnets always attract each other.
misconceptions.correction: Magnets do not always attract. Whether they attract or repel depends on which poles face each other. Like poles (N--N or S--S) repel and push apart; only unlike poles (N--S) attract. A child who has only seen a magnet pick up iron objects assumes magnets always pull things together, but two magnets can push each other apart when like poles face each other.

misconceptions.belief: Repulsion means the magnets are broken or weak.
misconceptions.correction: Repulsion is a normal and important behaviour of magnets -- it is not a sign of damage. In fact, observing repulsion is the surest test that both objects are magnets, because attraction can happen between a magnet and any magnetic material (like iron), but repulsion happens only between two magnets. CISCE examiner reports note that many candidates confuse the effect of pole orientation with the strength or condition of the magnet, so always attribute the behaviour to pole orientation, not to the magnet being "weak" or "faulty."

misconceptions.belief: The force between magnets requires them to touch.
misconceptions.correction: The magnetic force is a non-contact force -- it acts at a distance. You can feel the push or pull before the magnets touch, and the suspended-magnet activity proves this because the suspended magnet moves without being touched by the approaching magnet.

diagnosticQuestions.question: State the fundamental rule about attraction and repulsion between magnets, and explain what is meant by like poles and unlike poles.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The fundamental rule of magnetism is that like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Like poles are two poles of the same kind facing each other -- a north pole facing another north pole (N--N) or a south pole facing another south pole (S--S). When like poles face each other, the magnets push apart; this pushing force is called repulsion. Unlike poles are two poles of different kinds facing each other -- a north pole facing a south pole (N--S) or a south pole facing a north pole (S--N). When unlike poles face each other, the magnets pull together; this pulling force is called attraction. So a north pole attracts a south pole but repels another north pole, and a south pole attracts a north pole but repels another south pole. The force acts at a distance -- the magnets do not need to touch for the push or pull to be felt, which makes it a non-contact force.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Two bar magnets are placed end to end. The end of magnet A is marked N and the end of magnet B facing it is also marked N. Explain whether the magnets will attract or repel, and why.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The magnets will repel each other. Both facing ends are marked N, so this is a case of like poles facing each other -- a north pole facing another north pole. According to the fundamental rule of magnetism, like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Since both poles are the same (N--N), the magnets experience a repulsive force and push apart. You would feel an invisible cushion resisting you if you tried to push them together, and if one magnet were freely suspended it would twist or swing away from the approaching magnet. The force is a non-contact force, so this repulsion is felt before the magnets actually touch. If magnet B were turned around so that its S pole faced the N pole of magnet A, the situation would change to unlike poles and the magnets would attract instead. The key reasoning step is to identify the poles facing each other and then apply the rule: same poles -> repulsion, different poles -> attraction.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "If two magnets attract each other, both of them must be magnets, and if they repel each other, both must be magnets too, so attraction and repulsion are equally good tests for a magnet." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement is partially correct but misleading as a whole, and the comparison it draws between attraction and repulsion as tests for magnetism is flawed. It is true that if two objects repel each other, both must be magnets -- because repulsion occurs only between like poles of two magnets. A magnet can attract a magnetic material such as iron or steel without that material being a magnet itself, so attraction alone does not prove that the attracted object is a magnet. Therefore repulsion is the more reliable test for whether an object is a magnet: if an object repels a known magnet, it must itself be a magnet. However, attraction is not an equally reliable test, because a magnet attracts any magnetic material -- a steel paper clip, an iron nail, a cobalt disc -- none of which need be magnets. So the student is wrong to claim that attraction and repulsion are equally good tests. Repulsion is the surest test; attraction is suggestive but not conclusive. The balanced conclusion is that both forces arise from the same rule (like poles repel, unlike poles attract), but as diagnostic tools for identifying a magnet, repulsion is strictly more reliable than attraction. A good examiner expects a student to distinguish between "a magnet attracts magnetic materials" and "a magnet attracts another magnet's opposite pole," and to recognise that only repulsion confirms magnetism in both objects.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Describe the activity to demonstrate attraction and repulsion using two bar magnets, including how you would record your observations.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Suspend one bar magnet horizontally by a thread tied around its middle so that it can rotate freely; allow it to come to rest, which it will do pointing in the north--south direction. Mark its ends N and S. Take the second bar magnet and bring one of its poles near one end of the suspended magnet, close enough to feel the force but without touching. Observe what happens to the suspended magnet and record it. Repeat for all four combinations: N near N, N near S, S near N, and S near S. Record the observations in a table with three columns -- "Pole of approaching magnet," "Pole of suspended magnet facing it," and "Observation (attracts/repels)." The expected results are: N near N -> suspended magnet rotates away (repulsion); S near S -> rotates away (repulsion); N near S -> suspended magnet rotates towards the approaching magnet (attraction); S near N -> rotates towards (attraction). The activity demonstrates the rule that like poles repel and unlike poles attract, and it also shows that the magnetic force is a non-contact force because the suspended magnet moves without being touched.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple game or puzzle for a Class 6 student that uses the rule of attraction and repulsion between magnets, and explain how it teaches the concept.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Design a "Magnet Maze" game. Take a shallow cardboard box and draw a winding maze path on the top with a start point and a finish point. Place a small magnetic disc (the "runner") on the start point on top of the maze. Underneath the box, the player holds a bar magnet and moves it to guide the runner along the path without lifting it through the cardboard. The challenge is that at certain points along the maze, fixed magnets are glued under the cardboard with their poles marked. The player must choose which end of their guiding magnet to use: to push the runner past a fixed N pole, they must bring their N pole near it (like poles repel, pushing the runner away from the wall); to pull the runner towards a gate, they must bring their S pole near the runner's N pole (unlike poles attract). The game teaches the rule because the player must constantly decide, based on the marked poles, whether to use attraction (unlike poles) to pull or repulsion (like poles) to push. A scoring rubric rewards correct pole choices and penalises wrong ones, reinforcing that like poles repel and unlike poles attract. The game also demonstrates the non-contact nature of the force, since the guiding magnet works through the cardboard without touching the runner.

masteryCriteria: Can state the rule that like poles repel (N--N, S--S) and unlike poles attract (N--S, S--N); can predict whether two bar magnets will attract or repel based on the poles facing each other; can describe the suspended-magnet activity and record observations for all four pole combinations (N--N, N--S, S--N, S--S); can explain that the force between magnets is a non-contact force acting at a distance.

title: Magnetic compass and finding directions
subject: physics
definition: A magnetic compass is a small instrument used to find directions. It consists of a small magnetic needle pivoted at its centre so that it can rotate freely, enclosed in a circular casing marked with the four main directions -- north (N), south (S), east (E), and west (W). The needle is a tiny magnet with a north pole painted (usually red) and a south pole painted (usually blue or black). Because the needle is balanced on a sharp pivot, it can spin with very little friction and settle only when the forces on it balance. The compass needle aligns in a north-south direction due to the earth's magnetic field, with the red (north) end pointing roughly towards the geographic north. This happens because the earth itself behaves like a giant magnet, with its magnetic poles located near (but not exactly at) the geographic poles. The earth's magnetic south pole lies near the geographic north pole, and the earth's magnetic north pole lies near the geographic south pole; this is why the north pole of the compass needle is attracted towards the geographic north. To use a compass, you place it flat on a surface, wait for the needle to stop spinning, and read which way the red end points -- that direction is north. Once north is known, the other three main directions follow: south is opposite north, east is to the right of north, and west is to the left of north. The four directions are marked on the compass dial at right angles to one another, with east at 90 degrees clockwise from north, south at 180 degrees, and west at 270 degrees. A magnetic compass is widely used by sailors, mountaineers, pilots, and trekkers to navigate when there are no roads, signposts, or landmarks -- for example, a sailor crossing the Arabian Sea from Mumbai to Muscat, or a trekker in the Himalayas near Manali, can use a compass to keep on course. The key idea is that the compass needle is simply a small magnet obeying the same magnetic property learned earlier -- a freely suspended magnet always settles in a north-south line -- but here the magnet is tiny and the "thing" pulling it is the earth's own magnetic field.
eli5: A magnetic compass is a tiny magnet on a pin inside a round box marked with N, S, E, and W. The magnet can spin freely, and because the earth itself is like a giant magnet, it pulls the little needle so that the red end always points north. Once you know north, south is behind you, east is to your right, and west is to your left. Sailors and trekkers carry it to find their way when there are no roads.

misconceptions.belief: The red end of the compass needle points to the geographic north pole because the earth's magnetic north pole is there.
misconceptions.correction: The red (north) end of the needle is attracted towards the earth's magnetic south pole, which happens to lie near the geographic north pole. So the red end points roughly towards geographic north, but the cause is attraction to the earth's magnetic south pole near that point. CISCE examiners have repeatedly observed that students confuse the direction of magnetic quantities and fail to use correct notation -- naming the poles correctly avoids this error.

misconceptions.belief: The compass needle points to the exact geographic north pole.
misconceptions.correction: The needle aligns with the earth's magnetic field, whose magnetic poles are near but not exactly at the geographic poles. There is a small difference called magnetic declination, but that is a Class 7 topic -- at Class 6 level, simply state that the red end points roughly north because of the earth's magnetic field.

misconceptions.belief: The compass needle stops spinning because it is tired or because of friction.
misconceptions.correction: The needle stops because the turning force on it becomes zero when it is aligned with the earth's magnetic field in a north-south line. The pivot reduces friction so the needle can settle accurately; friction is not what stops it in the desired direction.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Describe a magnetic compass and state why its needle settles in a north-south direction.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A magnetic compass is a small instrument consisting of a tiny magnetic needle pivoted at its centre so that it can rotate freely, enclosed in a circular casing marked with the four main directions -- north (N), south (S), east (E), and west (W). The north-seeking end of the needle is painted red and the south-seeking end is painted blue or black. When the compass is placed flat and the needle is allowed to spin, it always settles in a north-south line with the red end pointing roughly towards the geographic north. This happens because the needle is a small magnet, and the earth itself behaves like a giant magnet with its magnetic poles near the geographic poles. The earth's magnetic field exerts a force on the tiny needle, twisting it until its north pole points along the field direction. A freely suspended magnet always aligns in a north-south direction -- the same property studied earlier with bar magnets -- and the compass needle is simply a very small, freely pivoted magnet obeying that rule. The pivot minimises friction so the needle can turn until the magnetic torque on it becomes zero, which is when it lies along the north-south line.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student places a magnetic compass on a table and the red end points towards a window. Explain how the student can now identify all four main directions, and why the needle points that way.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The red end of the compass needle always points towards the north, so the direction of the window is north. Once north is known, the other three directions are found by their fixed positions relative to north. South is directly opposite north -- so if the student turns around to face away from the window, they are facing south. East is 90 degrees to the right of north -- so the student's right side (while facing the window) is east. West is 90 degrees to the left of north -- so the student's left side (while facing the window) is west. The reason the red end points north is that the needle is a small magnet pivoted at its centre, and the earth behaves like a giant magnet whose magnetic south pole lies near the geographic north pole. The north pole of the needle (the red end) is attracted towards the earth's magnetic south pole near the geographic north, so it settles pointing roughly north. The earth's magnetic field exerts a turning force on the needle until it aligns along the north-south line, where the force becomes balanced and the needle stops.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A classmate claims that a magnetic compass will work perfectly anywhere in the world and will always point exactly to the geographic north pole. Evaluate this claim, stating what is correct and what is not.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The claim is partly correct but largely inaccurate, and a careful student should challenge both halves. The correct part is that a magnetic compass does work anywhere on the earth's surface, because the earth's magnetic field surrounds the whole planet and the compass needle is simply a small magnet responding to that field. So a compass is a reliable direction-finding tool on land, at sea, and in the air across the globe. However, the claim that the needle always points exactly to the geographic north pole is wrong. The compass needle aligns with the earth's magnetic field, and the earth's magnetic poles are near but not exactly at the geographic poles. There is a small angular difference between the direction the needle points (magnetic north) and the true geographic north, known as magnetic declination. This angle varies from place to place on the earth and is not the same everywhere. At Class 6 level we treat the red end as pointing "roughly north" and use it to find the four main directions, which is good enough for everyday navigation. But the precise statement -- that the needle points exactly to the geographic north pole -- is false, and the full study of this difference (magnetic declination, magnetic meridian) is reserved for Class 7. Therefore the classmate is right that a compass is a universal tool but wrong that it points exactly to geographic north; the needle follows the earth's magnetic field, not the geographic axis. A balanced answer should acknowledge the usefulness of the compass while correcting the overstatement about exact alignment.

diagnosticQuestions.question: You are standing in your school playground in Delhi with a magnetic compass. The red end of the needle points towards the school building. Identify the direction of the school building, the direction of the main gate if it is directly behind you, and the direction of the library if it is to your right. Explain your reasoning.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The red end of the compass needle always points towards the north, so the school building lies to the north of where you are standing. Since the main gate is directly behind you, and you are facing north towards the school building, the direction directly opposite north is south -- therefore the main gate is to the south. The library is to your right; when you face north, your right hand points to the east, so the library is to the east. The reasoning rests on the fixed arrangement of the four main directions around a person facing north: north is in front, south is behind, east is to the right, and west is to the left. On a compass dial these are spaced at 90-degree intervals -- east is a quarter turn clockwise from north, south is a half turn, and west is three-quarters of a turn. The compass works because its pivoted magnetic needle aligns with the earth's magnetic field, settling in a north-south line with the red (north) end pointing roughly towards the geographic north. Once that one direction (north) is fixed by the needle, the other three follow by their fixed relative positions, allowing you to orient yourself anywhere -- in a playground in Delhi, on a ship in the Arabian Sea, or on a trek in the Himalayas.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple classroom activity, using a magnetic compass, that helps your classmates find and label the four main directions of the classroom. Describe the steps and what you expect them to observe.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: I would organise the activity as follows. Step 1: Place a magnetic compass flat on a table in the centre of the classroom, away from large iron objects like cupboard doors or steel chairs, because nearby iron can disturb the needle. Step 2: Wait for about ten seconds so the needle stops spinning and settles. Step 3: Note the direction in which the red end of the needle points -- this is north. Step 4: Ask a classmate to stand beside the compass facing the same way as the red end; that classmate is now facing north. Step 5: Using chalk or sticky notes, label the wall in front of the classmate as "North". Step 6: Label the wall directly behind as "South", the wall to the classmate's right as "East", and the wall to the classmate's left as "West". Step 7: Rotate the compass gently and let go -- the needle should spin and then settle again in the same north-south line, showing that the alignment is caused by the earth's magnetic field, not by the way the compass is placed. Expected observations: the needle always comes to rest with the red end pointing the same way (north), no matter how the compass is turned beforehand; the four labelled directions stay fixed to the walls of the room; and classmates can verify the labels by checking that east is to the right of north and west is to the left. This activity demonstrates that a freely pivoted magnetic needle aligns with the earth's magnetic field and can be used to orient oneself and find the four main directions anywhere.

masteryCriteria: Can describe a magnetic compass as a small magnetic needle pivoted at its centre, free to rotate, enclosed in a casing marked with N, S, E, W; can explain that the compass needle aligns in a north-south direction because of the earth's magnetic field, with the red (north) end pointing north; can use a compass to identify the four main directions -- north, south, east, and west -- and state that south is opposite north, east is 90 degrees to the right of north, and west is 90 degrees to the left of north; can state that the earth behaves like a giant magnet with magnetic poles near the geographic poles.
